docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An Action is anything you do during an Encounter.

On your Turn, you can take 1 Normal Action, Bonus Action, Object Action, and Reaction, and you can take any number of Free Actions.

docs.title: Normal Actions
docs.text:
A Normal Action is the most common kind of Action.

The following Normal Actions are available to every creature, and some features add new ways to use them. You can also attempt an Action not listed here; the DM tells you whether it's possible and what roll, if any, it needs.

docs.title: Attack
docs.text: You make 1 Attack Roll with a Weapon or Unarmed Strike.

docs.title: Dash
docs.text: Your total movement increases by your Speed until the end of the Turn.

docs.title: Disengage
docs.text: Your movement doesn't trigger Opportunity Attacks until the end of the Turn.

docs.title: Dodge
docs.text: Creatures gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls against you, and you gain Advantage on Reflex Saves, until the start of your next Turn, you become Incapacitated, or your Speed becomes 0.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Choose an Ally or an Enemy within your Reach. The corresponding effect lasts until the start of your next Turn.

Ally Choose 1 of your Proficiencies; the Ally's next Ability Check that uses it gains Advantage. Enemy The next Attack Roll an Ally makes against the Enemy gains Advantage.

docs.title: Hide
docs.text: Make a Stealth Check. You become Hidden (DC the Stealth Check's total).

docs.title: Magic
docs.text: You use a Spell, feature, or item that produces a magical effect.

docs.title: Ready
docs.text:
Choose another Action and a perceivable trigger for it.

After the next time the trigger occurs before the start of your next Turn, you can take the chosen Action as a Reaction.

docs.title: Readying a Dash
docs.text: If you Ready a Dash, you can move using the extra movement as part of the Reaction.

docs.title: Readying Magic
docs.text: If you Ready a Magic Action, you Concentrate until you take the readied Action. If your Concentration breaks, you can't take the readied Action, but you don't expend the Spell Slot or the Action's other costs.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Make a Wisdom Check to notice something that isn't obvious. What you're looking for determines the Skill that applies:

Insight A creature's state of mind Perception A hidden creature or object Survival Tracks, food, or a Beast's state of mind

docs.title: Study
docs.text:
Make an Intelligence Check to recall or discern a piece of knowledge. The subject sets the Skill that applies:

Arcana Spells, Magic Items, planes, or magical creatures History Civilizations, historic events and people, wars, or long-lived creatures Medicine Ailments, anatomy, diseases, or treatments Nature Terrain, plants, weather, or natural creatures Religion Deities, rites, holy symbols, cults, or Celestial and Fiendish creatures

docs.title: Utilize
docs.text: You interact with one nonmagical object or environmental effect.

docs.title: Bonus Actions
docs.text: A Bonus Action is especially quick, and can only be taken when a feature or effect lets you. You can also spend a Normal Action to take a Bonus Action, but you can't take the same Bonus Action more than once per Turn.

docs.title: Object Actions
docs.text: An Object Action lets you interact with one nonmagical object or environmental effect that doesn't require the Utilize Action — such as drawing a weapon, opening a door, picking up an item, or handing an item to another creature. You can also Utilize to take an additional Object Action.

docs.title: Reactions
docs.text:
A Reaction is taken in response to a trigger, and each Spell or feature that uses one states its trigger.

Unlike other Actions, you can take a Reaction on any creature's Turn, but you can take only one Reaction until the start of your next Turn. If your Reaction interrupts another creature's Turn, that Turn resumes right after the Reaction.

docs.title: Opportunity Attacks
docs.text: An Opportunity Attack is an attack made as a Reaction, and can only by taken when a feature or effect lets you.

docs.title: Free Actions
docs.text: A Free Action requires no serious effort, and can only be taken when a feature or effect lets you.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: A Condition temporarily alters a creature's capabilities.

docs.title: Stacking Conditions
docs.text:
The same Condition can be applied by several effects at once.

Some Condition effects compound, while others play out the same no matter how many sources apply them. Either way, each source is tracked individually: a Condition lasts until every source that applied it has ended, and an effect that removes a Condition may remove one or all of its sources at once.

Many Conditions build on others; for example, a creature that is Paralyzed is also Incapacitated and Restrained, and has every effect of those Conditions. Defenses against an effect of a Condition don't extend to the Condition.

docs.title: Anchored
docs.text:
• You are Immobile.
  • You can't be moved by any effect.
  • You can't be knocked Prone (If you are already prone, you remain prone).
  • You automatically fail Reflex Saves.

docs.title: Asleep
docs.text: • You are Unconscious.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you take damage, or after a creature with you within its Reach Utilizes to wake you.

docs.title: Bleeding
docs.text:
The effect that causes this condition sets a Bleed Die.

  • After your Turn starts, you take a roll of the Bleed Die as Slashing Damage, and the number of Bleed Dice you roll increases by 1.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you heal.

docs.title: Blinded
docs.text:
• You can't see.
  • You automatically fail Ability Checks that require sight
  • You gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls.
  • Creatures gain Advantage on Attack Rolls against you.

docs.title: Burning
docs.text:
The effect that causes this condition sets a Burn Die.

  • After your Turn starts, you take a roll of the Burn Die as Fire Damage.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you spend 15 feet of movement while Prone, or after the fire is doused or submerged.

docs.title: Charmed
docs.text:
• You can't target the source of the Charm with harmful Attacks, features, or Spells.
  • The source of the Charm gains Advantage on Ability Checks to interact with you socially.

docs.title: Corroding
docs.text:
The effect that causes this condition sets a Caustic Die.

  • After your Turn starts, you take a roll of the Caustic Die as Acid Damage.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after 1 minute, or after you are doused or submerged in clean water or a neutralizing substance.

docs.title: Dazed
docs.text:
• On your Turn, you can either Move or take an Action, not both.
  • You can take a Bonus Action only by spending a Normal Action.
  • You can't take Reactions.

docs.title: Deafened
docs.text:
• You can't hear.
  • You automatically fail Ability Checks that require hearing.

docs.title: Downed
docs.text:
A player character or a named NPC is Downed at 0 Hit Points. Any other creature dies.

  • You are Dazed and Prone.
  • Your Concentration is broken.
  • You drop anything you're holding.
  • Before you take an Action, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 11); on a failure, the Action has no effect.
  • After your Turn starts, you make a Death Save.
  • After you take damage, you fail a Death Save — or two if the damage is from a Critical Hit.

docs.title: Death Saves
docs.text:
A Death Save has a DC of 11 and adds no Ability.

  • On a roll of 1 it counts as two failures.
  • On a roll of 20 you instead heal 1 Hit Point.

After you fail 3 Death Saves, you die. After you succeed on 3, you become Stable.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text:
This condition ends after you become Stable or have more than 0 Hit Points, and you remain Prone when it ends.

A creature that can Reach you can Utilize to make a Medicine Check (DC 10); on a success, you become Stable.

docs.title: Drifting
docs.text:
Drifting has a distance and a direction.

  • After your Turn starts, you are moved that distance in that direction.
  • You can't Move, but you can spend your movement to reduce the Drifting distance — each foot spent reduces it by 1 foot.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after the distance reaches 0.

docs.title: Exhausted
docs.text:
Exhaustion is tracked in levels.

  • Each time you become Exhausted, you gain 1 Exhaustion level.
  • You die if you reach 6 Exhaustion levels.
  • Before you make a d20 roll, you reduce the total by twice your Exhaustion level.
  • Your Speed decreases by 5 feet for each Exhaustion level.
  • After you finish a Long Rest, you remove 1 Exhaustion level.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you have no Exhaustion levels.

docs.title: Frightened
docs.text:
• While you can see the source of the Fear, you gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls and Ability Checks.
  • You can't willingly Move closer to the source.

docs.title: Grappled
docs.text:
• You are Immobile.
  • You gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls against any creature other than the grappler.
  • The grappler can propel you with it when it Moves, but each foot of that movement costs it 1 extra foot unless you are Tiny or at least 2 Sizes smaller than it.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you leave the grappler's Reach.

docs.title: Hidden
docs.text:
The effect that causes this condition sets a Hide DC. A creature whose Passive Perception exceeds your Hide DC ignores this condition.

  • Other creatures don't know your location.
  • You gain Advantage on Initiative Checks and Attack Rolls.
  • Creatures gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls against you.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text:
This condition ends after:

  • you make an Attack Roll.
  • you cast a Spell with Verbal components.
  • an Enemy sees you.
  • an Enemy uses the Search action and its total exceeds your Hide DC.

docs.title: Immobile
docs.text:
• Your Speed is 0 and can't change.
  • You gain Disadvantage on Reflex Saves.

docs.title: Incapacitated
docs.text:
• You can't take Actions, Bonus Actions, or Reactions.
  • You can't speak.
  • Your Concentration is broken.

docs.title: Invisible
docs.text:
• You and anything you're wearing or carrying can't be seen.
  • You gain Advantage on Attack Rolls.
  • Creatures gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls against you.

docs.title: Marked
docs.text: Marked has no effect on its own. It marks a creature as the target of an ongoing effect so that effect can track it; the feature or Spell that applies this condition defines what it does and when it ends.

docs.title: Paralyzed
docs.text:
• You are Incapacitated and Restrained.
  • Before you are hit by an attack while the attacker is within 5 feet, that attack becomes a Critical Hit.

docs.title: Petrified
docs.text:
• You are Incapacitated and Restrained.
  • You are Blinded, Deafened, and unaware of your surroundings.
  • You gain Resistance to all damage.
  • You and nonmagical objects you are wearing or carrying turn into a solid, inanimate substance, usually stone.
  • Your weight is multiplied by 10.
  • You stop aging.

docs.title: Prone
docs.text:
• Each foot you Move costs 1 extra foot.
  • You gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls and Reflex Saves.
  • Creatures gain Advantage on Attack Rolls against you while within 5 feet, and Disadvantage otherwise.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you spend half your Speed to stand up.

docs.title: Restrained
docs.text:
• You are Immobile.
  • You automatically fail Reflex Saves.
  • You gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls.
  • Creatures gain Advantage on Attack Rolls against you.

docs.title: Sickened
docs.text: • You gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls and Ability Checks.

docs.title: Stable
docs.text:
• You are Dazed.
  • Before you take an Action, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 11); on a failure, the Action has no effect.
  • After 1d4 hours pass, you heal 1 Hit Point.
  • After you take damage, you are Downed, and you also fail a Death Save if the damage is from a Critical Hit.

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after you are Downed or have more than 0 Hit Points.

docs.title: Stunned
docs.text: • You are Incapacitated and Restrained.

docs.title: Unconscious
docs.text:
• You are Incapacitated, Restrained, and Prone (you remain Prone when Unconscious ends).
  • You are Blinded and Deafened.
  • You drop anything you're holding.
  • Before you are hit by an attack while the attacker is within 5 feet, that attack becomes a Critical Hit.

docs.title: Withering
docs.text:
The effect that causes this condition sets a Wither Die.

  • After your Turn starts, you take a roll of the Wither Die as Necrotic Damage, and your Hit Point Maximum decreases by that amount (your Hit Point Maximum doesn't increase when Withing ends).

docs.title: Ending the Condition
docs.text: This condition ends after 1 minute.

docs.title: Encounters
docs.text: An Encounter is any scene where timing matters.

docs.title: Initiative
docs.text: Initiative is the order participants in an Encounter take Turns until the Encounter is resolved.

docs.title: Initiative Checks
docs.text: When an Encounter begins, each participant makes an Initiative Check to set the order of Turns, from highest result to lowest. An Initiative Check adds your Dexterity to the total.

docs.title: Initiative Ties
docs.text: If multiple Initiative Checks tie, the creature with the higher Dexterity goes first. If they still tie, each tied creature rolls a d20, and the higher roll goes first.

docs.title: Rounds
docs.text: A Round is about 6 seconds, and each participant takes one Turn per Round. Once every participant has taken a Turn, the Encounter moves to the next Round, and continues Round by Round until the Encounter ends.

docs.title: Combat
docs.text: Combat is an encounter that involves fighting. Combat begins when an Enemy in an encounter becomes aware of you, and ends after no Enemies remain.

docs.title: Hazards
docs.text: A Hazard is one of the many natural dangers while adventuring.

docs.title: Air Quality
docs.text:
There are three levels of Air Quality.

Air Quality Effect Fresh Air Breathable; no effect. Foul Air You are Sickened while you breathe it. Deadly Air Unbreathable; you begin suffocating.

docs.title: Dehydration
docs.text: A Medium Humanoid needs 1 gallon of water per day. Each Day you go without water, you are exhausted. Until you drink a full day's water, you can't remove Exhaustion and you can't benefit from a Rest.

docs.title: Rationing Water
docs.text: Each Day you drink half as much water, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 15); on a failure, you are exhausted. Either way, you still suffer Dehydration's other effects.

docs.title: Extreme Cold
docs.text:
After each hour you're exposed to temperatures 0 degrees Fahrenheit or lower, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 10); on a failure, you are exhausted.

  • Each time you make this Saving Throw, the DC increases by 5 until you complete a Long Rest.
  • If you gain Cold Resistance, you automatically succeed.

docs.title: Extreme Heat
docs.text:
After each hour you're exposed to temperatures 100 degrees Fahrenheit or higher, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 15); on a failure, you are exhausted.

  • Creatures wearing Medium or Heavy armor gain Disadvantage.
  • Creatures that drink at least half a gallon of water gain Advantage.
  • Each time you make this Saving Throw, the DC increases by 5 until you complete a Long Rest.
  • If you gain Fire Resistance, you automatically succeed.

docs.title: Sleep Deprivation
docs.text: Resting isn't mandatory, but going without sleep has consequences. Each day you go without finishing a Travel Rest or Long Rest, you make a Fortitude Save (DC 10); on a failure, you are exhausted. Each time you make this Saving Throw, the DC increases by 5 until you complete a Long Rest.

docs.title: Starvation
docs.text: A Medium Humanoid needs 1 pound of food per day. You can go without food for 3 + CON days (minimum 1 day). Each Day beyond that, you are exhausted. Until you eat a full day's food, you can't remove Exhaustion and you can't benefit from a Rest. A normal day of eating reduces the count of days without food by 1.

docs.title: Rationing Food
docs.text: Eating at least half as much food is enough to stave off Starvation temporarily. Each Day you do, you aren't exhausted, but you still suffer Starvation's other effects and it doesn't reset the number of days without food.

docs.title: Suffocation
docs.text: You can hold your breath for 1 + CON minutes (minimum 30 seconds). After your air runs out, you can survive for a number of Rounds equal to CON (minimum 1 Round). After your next Turn starts, you drop to 0 Hit Points and are Downed, and you can't regain Hit Points or become Stable until you can breathe again.

docs.title: Movement
docs.text: Movement is how a character gets from place to place using its Speed.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
Your Speed is the maximum distance you can move on a Turn.

A creature can have additional Speeds that let it ignore normal movement restrictions. You can switch between your Speeds as you Move, but the distance you travel using each Speed can't exceed that Speed's maximum, and your total movement in a Turn can't exceed the largest Speed you used that Turn.

docs.title: Splitting Movement
docs.text: You can move before and after any Action on your Turn. However you break it up, your total movement that Turn can't exceed your Speed.

docs.title: Dropping Prone
docs.text: You can drop Prone without spending an Action or any movement, unless your Speed is 0.

docs.title: Difficult Terrain
docs.text: Difficult Terrain is hard to move through. Each foot you move through or out of Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot.

docs.title: Squeezing
docs.text: Spaces sized for creatures 1 Size smaller than you are Difficult Terrain. You can't move through smaller spaces.

docs.title: Moving Through Creatures
docs.text:
You can move freely through the space of Allies and Tiny creatures. You can also move through the space of Incapacitated creatures and creatures at least 2 Sizes larger or smaller than you, but that space is Difficult Terrain.

You can't willingly end your move in another creature's space. If you end your Turn in a space with another creature, the smaller creature is knocked Prone, unless either is Tiny (If you are both the same size, both are knocked Prone).

docs.title: Burrowing
docs.text: Burrowing is moving through soft ground, such as earth, sand, or mud. A Burrow Speed lets you burrow, otherwise burrowing requires significant tools and time to make progress.

docs.title: Climbing
docs.text: Climbing is moving across vertical surfaces. You need both hands, and each foot you move costs 1 extra foot. A Climb Speed lets you climb without that extra cost.

docs.title: Spider Climbing
docs.text: A Spider Climb Speed is a Climb Speed, and you can also climb with your hands free and move along ceilings upside down.

docs.title: Falling
docs.text:
Falling forces you to move when you are airborne with no way to stay aloft. Falling doesn't cost any movement.

Each time you fall, you fall up to 500 feet until you land or gain a way to stay aloft. After your Turn starts, if you are still falling, you fall another 500 feet.

While falling, anything you collide with makes a Reflex Save (DC 15).

Fail You and whatever you struck take 1d6 Bludgeoning damage for every 10 feet you fell and are knocked Prone. The next time you collide with something, the damage is calculated from this location, not the total distance you fell. Success You continue moving until you strike something else or have moved the total falling distance.

docs.title: Flying
docs.text: Flying is moving through the air. A Fly Speed lets you fly, but you fall if you are Incapacitated or Prone, or if your Fly Speed is 0.

docs.title: Hovering
docs.text: A Hover Speed is a Fly Speed, and you gain Drifting and Prone Immunity, and you don't fall if you are Incapacitated or your Fly Speed is 0.

docs.title: Jumping
docs.text:
Jumping is moving horizontally or vertically, avoiding most terrain effects. Your Strength determines how far or high you can jump, and each foot you jump costs 1 foot of movement.

If you don't move at least 10 feet in a straight line immediately before a jump, the distance you can jump is halved.

docs.title: Long Jump
docs.text: You can cover a horizontal distance up to (5 × STR) + 10 feet.

docs.title: High Jump
docs.text: You can cover a vertical distance up to 3 + STR feet. During the jump, you can extend your arms to reach up to half your height higher.

docs.title: Propelled
docs.text:
Propelled movement forces you to move against your will. Being propelled doesn't cost any movement.

While propelled, anything you collide with makes a Reflex Save (DC 15).

Fail You and whatever you struck take 1d6 Bludgeoning damage for every 10 feet of propelled movement you had remaining and are knocked Prone. Then, you stop being propelled. Success You continue moving until you strike something else or have moved the total propelled distance.

docs.title: Swimming
docs.text: Swimming is moving through liquid. You need both hands, and each foot you move costs 1 extra foot. A Swim Speed lets you swim without that extra cost.

docs.title: Resting
docs.text: Rest is the time it takes to recover from fatigue and lingering injuries.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: You must begin a Rest with at least 1 Hit Point and do nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, dozing, or standing watch. After you finish a Rest, you must wait at least twice its duration before starting another Rest of the same kind.

docs.title: Interruptions
docs.text: A Rest ends early if you roll Initiative, cast a Spell other than a Cantrip, take damage, walk for 1 hour, or exert yourself physically. You can resume a Rest immediately, but each interruption adds 1 hour to the time a Travel Rest or Long Rest needs to finish.

docs.title: Short Rest
docs.text: A Short Rest takes 1 hour.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text: After you finish a Short Rest, you can spend Hit Dice to heal: for each Hit Die you spend, you heal by HD + CON. You can choose to spend another Hit Die after each roll.

docs.title: Travel Rest
docs.text: A Travel Rest takes 4 hours: at least 3 hours of sleep and no more than 1 hour of light activity.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text: After you finish a Travel Rest, you gain the effect of a Short Rest and regain up to half your total Hit Dice.

docs.title: Long Rest
docs.text: A Long Rest takes 8 hours: at least 6 hours of sleep and no more than 2 hours of light activity.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
After you finish a Long Rest:

  • you heal all lost Hit Points.
  • you regain all spent Hit Dice.
  • you restore any reduced Hit Point Maximum and Abilities.
  • your Exhaustion level reduces by 1.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Time is typically measured in seconds, minutes, and hours within a single adventuring day.

docs.title: The Day
docs.text:
A Day is the fundamental recurring time cycle of a setting. Its length and starting moment are set by the DM based on context; typically a 24-hour cycle beginning at a fixed point such as midnight or dawn, or an equivalent cycle in a setting where time works differently, such as the Astral Plane.

Features and Magic Items that recharge each Day do so at the start of each Day, independent of any creature's Rest. If a Day starts during an Encounter, the recharge waits until the Encounter ends.

Unit Length (in Days) Day 1 Week 5 Tenday 10 Month 30

docs.title: Difficulty Class
docs.text:
Ability Checks and Saving Throws use a Difficulty Class to determine success. The Difficulty Class is set by the effect that required the dice roll, or by the Dungeon Master.

Attack Rolls use the target's Armor Class to determine success instead.

docs.title: Choosing to Fail
docs.text: You can choose to fail an Ability Check or a Saving Throw, or to be hit by an Attack.

docs.title: Advantage / Disadvantage
docs.text:
You gain Advantage or Disadvantage on a Dice Roll when a circumstance favors or hinders you. Either way, roll the dice twice:

  • with Advantage, use the higher total.
  • with Disadvantage, use the lower total.

You can only gain Advantage or Disadvantage before the dice are rolled. Gaining either after the dice are rolled has no effect.

docs.title: Stacking Advantage
docs.text: No matter how many times you gain Advantage or Disadvantage on a Dice Roll, you still roll only twice.

docs.title: Stacking Together
docs.text: You can't have both Advantage and Disadvantage on a Dice Roll. If you would have both, count how many times you gained each. You keep whichever you gained more, and lose the other. If the counts are equal, you have neither on that roll.

docs.title: Rerolls
docs.text: A Reroll lets you roll a die again, replacing the old result.

docs.title: Rerolling with Advantage / Disadvantage
docs.text: Advantage and Disadvantage resolve as soon as the dice are rolled, leaving the roll with a single d20. A later reroll or replacement acts on that die alone, and can itself have Advantage or Disadvantage if the effect granting it says so.

docs.title: Proficiency
docs.text:
Proficiency measures how much a creature's training improves its rolls. Each Proficiency has a tier that sets how much of your Proficiency Bonus applies to it.

Tier Proficiency Bonus Aptitude half, rounded up Proficiency full Expertise double

docs.title: Proficiency Bonus
docs.text: When you make a roll you're Proficient with, you add your Proficiency Bonus to it. Your Proficiency Bonus is determined by your Level.

docs.title: Applying Proficiency
docs.text:
Most Proficiencies add your Proficiency Bonus to a related roll.

Proficiency Adds your Bonus to Skill Ability Checks that use the Skill Trade Ability Checks that use the Trade Saving Throw Saving Throws of that type Weapon Attack Rolls with the Weapon Armor Armor Class Shield —

docs.title: Weapons
docs.text: Proficiency with a Weapon is tied to its specific type, or a broader category: Simple or Martial, and Melee or Ranged.

docs.title: Armor
docs.text:
Proficiency with Armor is tied to its weight: Light, Medium, or Heavy. A Shield uses the Armor Proficiency of its weight.

Unlike other Proficiencies, Armor Proficiency adds your Proficiency Bonus to your Armor Class rather than to a roll. Wearing Armor or wielding a Shield you aren't Proficient with grants no benefit, but carries no penalty.

docs.title: Stacking Proficiencies
docs.text: You can apply only one Proficiency to a single roll; if an Ability Check uses both a Skill and a Trade you're Proficient with, you gain Advantage on it instead.

docs.title: Attack Rolls
docs.text: An Attack Roll determines the outcome when you attempt to hit a creature with a weapon or Spell.

docs.title: 1. Declare the attack.
docs.text: Choose a target within your attack's Range.

docs.title: 2. Determine modifiers.
docs.text: Abilities, Proficiency, Cover, and other effects can add bonuses, penalties, Advantage, or Disadvantage to the Attack Roll.

docs.title: 3. Determine if the attack hits.
docs.text: Roll the d20 and add your modifiers. If the total equals or exceeds the target's Armor Class, the attack hits. If the number on the die equals or exceeds your Critical Hit Range, the attack is a Critical Hit.

docs.title: 4. Resolve the attack's effects.
docs.text: After an Attack hits, you usually make a Damage Roll. The weapon, Spell, or feature you used describes the Damage Dice and the Damage Type.

docs.title: Armor Class
docs.text: Armor Class measures how difficult it is to land an attack on a creature. Most Humanoids wear Armor to improve their defenses, while other creatures can have Natural Armor.

docs.title: Types of Attacks
docs.text:
Every attack is a Weapon or Spell attack, and either Melee or Ranged. These qualities set the attack's Range and the Ability you add to its Attack Roll and Damage Roll.

Attack Range Attack Ability Damage Ability Melee Weapon your Reach Strength Strength Ranged Weapon the weapon's range Dexterity Dexterity Melee Spell your Reach Spellcasting Ability — Ranged Spell the effect's Range Spellcasting Ability —

docs.title: Ranged Attacks
docs.text: A Ranged Attack lists its range in feet. The first number is the Normal Range; a second number, if any, is the Long Range. You can't hit a target outside of the largest Range listed.

docs.title: Range Penalty
docs.text: Ranged Attacks against a target beyond Normal Range, but within Long Range, gain Disadvantage.

docs.title: Melee Penalty
docs.text: While you are within an Enemy's Reach, you gain Disadvantage on Ranged Attacks.

docs.title: Nonlethal Attacks
docs.text: You can declare any Melee attack as Nonlethal when you make it. If a Nonlethal attack reduces the target to 0 Hit Points, the target becomes Stable instead of Downed.

docs.title: Critical Hits
docs.text: You score a Critical Hit when you roll a 20 on the d20 for an Attack Roll.

docs.title: Critical Hit Range
docs.text: The minimum number to score a Critical Hit decreases each time your Critical Hit Range increases.

docs.title: NPC Critical Hits
docs.text: For an unnamed NPC, a Critical Hit maximizes the attack's Damage Roll: each Damage Die is treated as rolling its highest value.

docs.title: Player Critical Hits
docs.text:
After a player or named NPC rolls a Critical Hit, choose 1 of the Damage Types the attack would deal and roll an additional d20. The Damage Type determines whether you gain Advantage on the additional d20, and what Condition, if any, the Critical Hit applies. The d20 roll sets the Critical Hit's damage, Condition Duration, and Condition Die.

A Condition from a Critical Hit lasts no longer than the roll's duration. Before their turn ends, a creature with a feature that can automatically succeed on a Saving Throw (such as Legendary Resistance or Indomitable) can use it to end the condition early.

Damage Type Advantage Against... Critical Condition Major Condition Bludgeoning Heavy Armor Dazed Stunned Piercing Medium Armor Immobile Restrained Slashing Unarmored, Light Armor Bleeding Bleeding Acid Constructs Corroding Corroding Cold Oozes Immobile Restrained Fire Beasts, Plants Burning Burning Lightning Medium Armor, Heavy Armor Immobile Paralyzed Poison Giants, Humanoids Sickened Paralyzed Thunder Elementals Dazed Stunned Force — Incapacitated Stunned Necrotic Celestials Withering Paralyzed Psychic Beasts, Monstrosities Frightened Unconscious Radiant Fiends, Undead Blinded Stunned Critical d20 Damage Condition Duration Bleed / Wither Die Burn / Caustic Die 1-10 Max — — — 11-15 Max + Roll 1 Round 1d8 1d8 16-17 Max + Roll 2 Rounds 1d8 2d6 18-19 2 × Max 2 Rounds 1d8 2d6 20 2 × Max 3 Rounds 1d10 2d10

docs.title: Major Critical Hit
docs.text:
After you roll a 20 on the Critical Hit Table, roll again on the Major Critical Hit Table, keeping Advantage if the Damage Type is effective. Its damage, duration, and Condition are added to the Critical Hit (each condition applied keeps its own duration).

Major d20 Damage Condition Duration Bleed / Wither Die Burn / Caustic Die 1-10 — 1 Round 1d8 1d8 11-15 +Roll 1 Round 1d8 1d8 16-17 +Roll 2 Rounds 1d8 2d6 18-19 +Max 3 Rounds 1d10 2d10 20 Drop to 0 HP — — —

docs.title: Ability Checks
docs.text: An Ability Check determines the outcome when you attempt something with a chance of failure (other than an attack).

docs.title: 1. Declare the Ability Check.
docs.text: Describe what you're attempting to do.

docs.title: 2. Determine modifiers.
docs.text: Abilities, Proficiency, and other effects can add bonuses, penalties, Advantage, or Disadvantage to the Ability Check.

docs.title: 3. Determine if the Ability Check succeeds.
docs.text: Roll the d20 and add your modifiers. If the total equals or exceeds the Difficulty Class, the Ability Check succeeds.

docs.title: 4. Resolve the Ability Check's effects.
docs.text: The effect that required the Ability Check, or the DM, determines what effects succeeding or failing has.

docs.title: Types of Ability Checks
docs.text: Most Ability Checks involve some type of Proficiency; usually a Skill or Trade.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills are areas of training that apply to Ability Checks.

Each Skill has a default Ability, but circumstances can pair a Skill with a different Ability — such as using Strength instead of Charisma to intimidate a creature.

Ability Skills Strength Athletics Dexterity Acrobatics, Precision, Stealth Constitution — Intelligence Arcana, History, Medicine, Nature, Religion Wisdom Insight, Perception, Survival Charisma Deception, Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion

docs.title: Passive Checks
docs.text:
A Passive Check represents the average result of a repeated task, or lets the DM secretly resolve an Ability Check. A Passive Check doesn't require a roll: your total is 10 plus every bonus that normally applies to the Ability Check.

If you have Advantage on the Ability Check, the Passive Check increases by 5. Likewise, if you have Disadvantage, it decreases by 5.

docs.title: Defenses
docs.text: Several defenses change how you make Ability Checks.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text: While you gain Protection against something, you gain Advantage on Ability Checks and Saving Throws you make to resist its effects.

docs.title: Immunity
docs.text: While you gain Immunity to something, you ignore all its effects, including Damage and Conditions.

docs.title: Damage Rolls
docs.text: A Damage Roll determines how much damage an effect deals.

docs.title: 1. Determine modifiers.
docs.text: Abilities, Resistance, Vulnerability and other effects can add bonuses, penalties, Advantage, or Disadvantage to the Damage Roll.

docs.title: 2. Apply the damage.
docs.text: Roll the Damage Dice and add the modifiers. You reduce the target's Hit Points by the total (minimum 0).

docs.title: Hit Points
docs.text: Hit Points represent a creature's physical health, luck, stamina, and resolve. When you take damage, you lose that many Hit Points; when you heal, you regain them, up to your Hit Point Maximum.

docs.title: Reaching 0 Hit Points
docs.text: At 0 Hit Points, a player character or a named NPC is Downed. Any other creature dies.

docs.title: Temporary Hit Points
docs.text: Temporary Hit Points are wells of additional health that prevent you from losing actual Hit Points until you finish a Long Rest. You can only have one pool of Temporary Hit Points at a time; if you gain Temporary Hit Points again, you choose 1 to keep.

docs.title: Bloodied
docs.text: While your Hit Points are half your Hit Point Maximum or lower, you are Bloodied. Being Bloodied has no effect on its own, but some effects grow stronger against a Bloodied creature or trigger when a creature becomes Bloodied.

docs.title: Hit Dice
docs.text: Your Hit Dice are a reserve of latent health. You can't draw on them freely — only certain effects let you spend or restore them, most often Resting.

docs.title: Damage Types
docs.text: Every instance of damage has a Damage Type. Damage Types have no rules of their own, but many other rules apply to a Damage Type or to its category.

docs.title: Additional Damage
docs.text: Some effects add damage to another source. If such an effect doesn't state a Damage Type, the additional damage uses the type of the source it adds to. When that source has more than one Damage Type, you choose which of those types the additional damage uses.

docs.title: Physical Damage
docs.text: Damage Type Examples Bludgeoning blunt objects, constriction, falling Piercing fangs, puncturing objects Slashing claws, cutting objects

docs.title: Elemental Damage
docs.text: Damage Type Examples Acid corrosive liquids, digestive enzymes Cold freezing water, icy blasts Fire flames, unbearable heat Lightning electricity Poison toxic gas, venom Thunder concussive sound

docs.title: Esoteric Damage
docs.text: Damage Type Examples Force pure magical energy Necrotic life-draining energy Psychic mind-rending energy Radiant holy energy, searing radiation

docs.title: Taking Damage
docs.text: Several defenses change how much damage a creature takes.

docs.title: Resistance
docs.text:
While you gain Resistance to something, you take half damage from its effects.

Resistance stacks with itself: two overlapping sources reduce the damage to a quarter, and three sources count as Immunity. Further sources have no additional effect.

docs.title: Vulnerability
docs.text:
While you gain Vulnerability to something, you take double damage from its effects.

Vulnerability stacks additively: each source adds the damage once more, rather than doubling it.

docs.title: Immunity
docs.text: While you gain Immunity to something, you ignore all its effects, including Damage and Conditions.

docs.title: Damage Reduction
docs.text: Before you take Physical Damage, you reduce it by your Damage Reduction (after any Resistance applies).

docs.title: Damage Threshold
docs.text: Before you take Damage, if that damage doesn't exceed your Damage Threshold (after all other modifiers have been applied), you take no Damage instead.

docs.title: Saving Throws
docs.text: An Saving Throw determines the outcome when you attempt to resist a Spell, trap, or other harmful effect.

docs.title: 1. Determine modifiers.
docs.text: Abilities, Proficiency, and other effects can add bonuses, penalties, Advantage, or Disadvantage to the Saving Throw.

docs.title: 2. Determine if the Saving Throw succeeds.
docs.text: Roll the d20 and add your modifiers. If the total equals or exceeds the Difficulty Class, the Saving Throw succeeds.

docs.title: 3. Resolve the Saving Throw's effects.
docs.text: The effect that required the Saving Throw determines what effects succeeding or failing has.

docs.title: Types of Saves
docs.text:
Most Saves are Fortitude, Reflex, or Will Saves.

Save Ability Fortitude Constitution Reflex Dexterity Will Wisdom

docs.title: Concentration Saves
docs.text: A Concentration Save determines whether you keep Concentration when you take damage. Concentration Saves use your Fortitude Save Proficiency.

docs.title: Death Saves
docs.text: A Death Save determines your fate while you are Downed.

docs.title: Defenses
docs.text: Several defenses change how you make Saving Throws.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text: While you gain Protection against something, you gain Advantage on Ability Checks and Saving Throws you make to resist its effects.

docs.title: Evasion
docs.text: While you gain Evasion against something, Saving Throws deal half damage to you when you fail, and no damage when you succeed.

docs.title: Immunity
docs.text: While you gain Immunity to something, you ignore all its effects, including Damage and Conditions.

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text: The Target of an attack or effect is whatever that effect acts upon.

docs.title: Choosing a Target
docs.text: Most effects involve choosing a target for the effect to act on.

docs.title: Targeting Yourself
docs.text: A "Self" target can only be you. Any other target can also be you, unless the effect says otherwise.

docs.title: Line of Effect
docs.text: You must have a clear path to a target, so it can't be behind Full Cover.

docs.title: Line of Sight
docs.text:
By default, you don't need to see something to choose it as a target.

If the unseen target isn't chosen as part of an Area, you gain Disadvantage on Attack Rolls made as part of the effect, and the target gains Advantage on Saving Throws against it.

docs.title: Worn or Held Objects
docs.text: You can target worn or held objects, such as Armor or a Weapon, unless the targets are chosen as part of an Area.

docs.title: Invalid Targets
docs.text: A target chosen for an effect that doesn't meet that effect's target requirements resolves normally, but the invalid target gains Immunity to the effect.

docs.title: Types of Targets
docs.text:
Every target is a Creature, an Object, a Location, or an Effect.

Target Description Creature A sentient being that acts under its own power. Object A physical thing that doesn't act under its own power. Location A place, rather than a thing. Other Effect A persistent effect from a spell, feature, or item.

Creatures and Objects both have a Size, an Armor Class, and Hit Points. What separates them is autonomy: a Creature decides what it does, and an Object doesn't.

docs.title: Animating
docs.text: An effect that animates an Object grants it that autonomy, changing it from an Object to a Creature for as long as the effect lasts.

docs.title: Creatures
docs.text:
A Creature acts under its own power. Most of the Compendium describes Creatures by default, so the rules governing them are collected elsewhere.

Rule Location Abilities, Checks, and Saves Dice Rolls Actions and Reactions Actions Speed and movement Movement Conditions Conditions Creature Type, Alignment, and Disposition Creature Codex

docs.title: Objects
docs.text: An Object doesn't act under its own power, and is usually used or affected by a Creature.

docs.title: Dice Rolls
docs.text: An Object has no Abilities, so it can't make an Attack, an Ability Check, or a Saving Throw under its own power. An Object required to make a Check or Save automatically fails it. What protects an Object is Immunity or Resistance, not the roll.

docs.title: Defenses
docs.text: An Object has Hit Points, an Armor Class and can have other defenses just as Creatures do. All Objects have Immunity to Poison and Psychic Damage.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: An Object can be affected by a Condition. Where a Condition would change something an Object doesn't have, that part of the Condition does nothing.

docs.title: Portions of an Object
docs.text: Some Objects are too large to have a single extent, such as a floor, a cliff face, or a castle wall. An effect on such an Object affects a portion of it, and only that portion is damaged or destroyed.

docs.title: Corpses
docs.text:
A Corpse is the body a Creature leaves behind when it dies. Death ends the autonomy that made it a Creature, so a Corpse is an Object.

A Corpse becomes a Creature again if it is restored to life, or if it is animated as an Undead.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
A Location is a place rather than a thing. It has no Size and no statistics, and can't be damaged. A Location required to make a Check or Save automatically fails it.

An effect that targets a Location affects that space. Anything in the space is affected only if the effect says so.

docs.title: Other Effects
docs.text:
Sometimes a Spell, or the effect of a Spell, Feature, or Item can be targeted directly.

While an effect is being activated, it fills the space of its source.

Once active, an effect fills the space of its Area, its targets, and any Creature or Object it conjured. An effect otherwise has no Size, no statistics, can't be damaged, and can't roll dice; the effect's source is usually required to roll instead.

docs.title: Conjuring
docs.text: An effect that conjures a Creature, an Object, or another effect creates it from magic. A conjured thing ceases to exist once the magic that conjured it ends.

docs.title: Cover
docs.text:
Cover is the protection a creature gains with an obstacle between itself and an attack.

Cover Effect Half Cover Your Armor Class and Reflex Saves increase by 2. Three-Quarters Cover Your Armor Class and Reflex Saves increase by 5. Full Cover You can't be seen or targeted directly by Attacks or Spells, and you automatically succeed on Reflex Saves.

There are three levels of Cover. If a target is behind multiple sources of Cover, only the strongest applies.

docs.title: Creatures and Objects as Cover
docs.text:
A creature or object between an effect's source and its target provides Cover to that target. How much it provides depends on their Sizes. A creature fills only part of its space, while an object fills its space more completely, so an object provides more Cover than a creature of the same Size.

Target's Size, compared to the obstacle Creature Object More than one Size larger None None One Size larger None Half Cover The same Size Half Cover Three-Quarters Cover Smaller Half Cover Full Cover

docs.title: Range and Areas
docs.text: An effect's Range is how far from its source it can reach, and an Area is the space that effect fills.

docs.title: Range
docs.text:
An effect's Range is how far from its source it can reach, given as a distance in feet or as a creature's Reach.

Once placed, an effect can extend beyond its Range, and movable effects aren't restricted by their source's Range unless their description says otherwise.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
An Area is a space an effect fills. Every Area has an Origin point and takes one of the following shapes:

Area Origin Measurement (ft.) Aura The creature or object it surrounds Radius Circle Its center Radius Cone Its apex Length; its width at any point equals that distance Cube The center of its near side Length of each side Cylinder The center of its base Radius × height Line Its near end Length × square cross-section width Sphere Its center Radius Square The center of its near side Length of each side Wall The center of its near side Length × width × height

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
An area's Origin is placed within its effect's Range. You choose where the Origin sits within that range, and once placed an Area can extend beyond it.

The Area extends from the Origin in straight lines, typically facing away from its source; Spheres instead face outwards from the Origin, and Cylinders face outwards from the top or bottom circle of the Area. If a straight line from the Origin to a location is blocked by Full Cover, that location is excluded from the Area.

docs.title: Auras
docs.text: An Aura is always fixed to its source's space, instead of a point. Auras are measured from the edges of that space, move with its source, and can include or exclude the source from its effect.

docs.title: Sight
docs.text: Sight covers what you can see, what blocks it, and the Senses that let you perceive beyond it.

docs.title: Obscurement
docs.text:
Obscurement is how well you can see into or through an area. Fog, foliage, and other visual obstacles can create different levels of Obscurement.

Obscurement Effect Clear You can see normally. Light You gain Disadvantage on Perception Checks that rely on sight. Heavy You are Blinded while trying to see into or through the area.

docs.title: Lighting
docs.text:
Lighting is the presence or absence of light in an area, which in turn affects its Obscurement. Lighting can make an area harder to see into, but not easier.

Lighting Effect Bright Light The area is Clear. Dim Light The area has Light Obscurement. Darkness The area has Heavy Obscurement.

docs.title: Sunlight
docs.text: Sunlight is a special type of naturally produced Light. Sunlight doesn't have any special rules of its own, but some effects only work in areas of Sunlight.

docs.title: Magical Darkness
docs.text: Magical Darkness is a special type of magically produced Darkness. Darkvision doesn't help you see through areas of Magical Darkness.

docs.title: Senses
docs.text:
Senses are the ways a creature perceives its surroundings beyond ordinary sight.

Most senses have a range, in feet; anything beyond that range is unaffected by the Sense. If you gain the same Sense from more than one effect, add their ranges together.

docs.title: Blindsight
docs.text: Blindsight lets you perceive your surroundings without relying on sight. You ignore the Blinded and Invisible conditions, and you ignore Half Cover and Three-Quarters Cover.

docs.title: Darkvision
docs.text: Darkvision lets you see in Dim Light as if it were Bright Light, and in Darkness as if it were Dim Light. You discern only shades of grey in that Darkness, not color.

docs.title: Devil's Sight
docs.text: Devil's Sight lets you see normally in Dim Light, Darkness, and Magical Darkness.

docs.title: Tremorsense
docs.text: Tremorsense lets you pinpoint the location of creatures and moving objects that are in contact with the same surface or liquid as you. This isn't a form of sight.

docs.title: Truesight
docs.text:
Truesight lets you see normally under most conditions. Within its range, you:

  • gain Blindsight.
  • gain Devil's Sight.
  • see visual illusions as translucent, and automatically succeed on Saving Throws against them.
  • see the true form of any creature or object transformed by magic.
  • can see into the Ethereal Plane.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
Every creature and object has a Size that describes the space it occupies or needs to move and fight effectively.

Category Rank Space (feet) Space (squares) Tiny 1 2.5 × 2.5 4 per square Small 2 5 × 5 1 × 1 Medium 3 5 × 5 1 × 1 Large 4 10 × 10 2 × 2 Huge 5 15 × 15 3 × 3 Gargantuan 6 20 × 20 or larger 4 × 4 or larger

Each Size has a Category that names it and a Rank that numbers it. An effect that raises or lowers a Size moves it that many Ranks, and an effect that compares two creatures measures the difference between their Ranks. A Size can't rise above Gargantuan or fall below Tiny.

docs.title: Using Spells
docs.text: Spells are magical effects used by Spellcasters and Magic Items.

docs.title: Spell Level
docs.text:
A Spell's Level, from 0 to 9, determines the minimum-level Spell Slot required to cast it. A Level 0 Spell is a Cantrip; Cantrips are always ready and never expend a Spell Slot.

Individual spells only have descriptions up to 6th-Level, but powerful Spellcasters can cast Spells beyond that, provided they have the Spell Slot to upcast it.

docs.title: Spell Level of non-Spell Effects
docs.text:
Each magical effect that isn't from a cast spell has a Spell Level based on its source (even if the effect names a Spell with a different Level).

Source Spell Level Feature creature's PB - 1 Common Item 0 Uncommon Item 1 Rare Item 3 Very Rare Item 5 Cursed/Legendary Item 7 Artifact 9

docs.title: Schools of Magic
docs.text:
A School of Magic groups Spells so other rules can reference them together; the Schools have no rules of their own. A Spell can belong to one or more Schools.

School Typical Effects Abjuration prevent or reverse harmful effects Conjuration transport creatures or objects Divination reveal information Enchantment influence minds Evocation channel energy into destructive effects Illusion deceive the mind or senses Necromancy manipulate life and death Transmutation transform creatures or objects

docs.title: Spell Lists
docs.text: Each class with a Spellcasting feature has its own Spell List, which determines the Spells that class can Prepare. A Spell belongs to every class whose List includes it.

docs.title: Gaining Spells
docs.text: How you gain a Spell determines how you cast it and whether you can change it later.

docs.title: Prepared Spells
docs.text: The Spellcasting feature lets you Prepare Spells from the class's Spell List; it sets how many you prepare, when you can change them, and how many at a time. You can't prepare a Spell if its Level is higher than the highest Spell Slot you have from the class you prepare it with.

docs.title: Learned Spells
docs.text: Features from your Race, Class, or Feats let you Learn Spells. A Spell learned from a Class Feature is also treated as though it were on that class's Spell List.

docs.title: Item Spells
docs.text: Some Items let you cast Spells through them; a Spell cast this way doesn't need to be Prepared or Learned.

docs.title: Spellcasting Ability
docs.text: Your Spellcasting Ability determines your Spell Attack modifier and your Spell Save DC. The way you cast a Spell sets which Ability you use as its Spellcasting Ability.

docs.title: Spell Slots
docs.text:
Casting a Spell usually expends a Spell Slot granted by the Spellcasting feature. Slots are leveled from 1 to 9.

To cast a Spell, you expend a Slot of the Spell's Level or higher. You can use your Spell Slots to cast any Spell you have Prepared or Learned.

docs.title: One Spell Slot per Turn
docs.text: You can expend only one Spell Slot to cast a Spell on each of your Turns. Spell Slots spent on other effects don't count against this limit.

docs.title: Upcasting
docs.text: When you cast a Spell using a Spell Slot higher than the Spell's Level, you Upcast it, and the Spell takes on the Level of the Slot for that casting. Some Spells have stronger effects when Upcast, described in the Spell's At Higher Levels section.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Spell Components are the words, gestures, and materials a caster must supply to cast a Spell. If you can't provide one or more of a Spell's Components, you can't cast it.

docs.title: Verbal
docs.text: A Verbal Component is a string of words spoken at a normal speaking voice. A Creature that can't speak, or that is within an area of magical silence, can't cast a Spell with a Verbal Component.

docs.title: Somatic
docs.text: A Somatic Component is a gesture performed with at least one hand.

docs.title: Material
docs.text:
A Material Component is an item used in the casting. You must have a free hand to access it, though it can be the same hand used for any Somatic Component.

If a Material Component is named, you must provide that specific item. The Spell states whether a named Component is consumed when the Spell is cast.

If a Material Component isn't named, you can use a Component Pouch. If you have the Spellcasting feature from a class the Spell belongs to, you can instead use the Spellcasting Focus described in that feature.

When you cast a Spell from an Item, the Item serves as the Spell's Material Component — even one that names a Component — and isn't consumed unless its description says otherwise.

docs.title: Casting Time
docs.text: Casting a Spell usually takes the Magic Action, but some Spells take a Bonus Action, a Reaction, or longer.

docs.title: Triggered Spells
docs.text: Every Spell with a Reaction Casting Time, and some Spells with a Bonus Action Casting Time, define a trigger that must occur before you can cast the Spell.

docs.title: Rituals
docs.text: A Spell with a Ritual Casting Time can be cast as normal or cast as a Ritual. Casting it as a Ritual takes 10 minutes longer and expends no Spell Slot.

docs.title: Long Casting Times
docs.text: Some Spells — including Spells cast as a Ritual — take 1 minute or longer to cast. While casting a Spell this way, you must maintain Concentration and take the Magic Action on each of your Turns to keep casting it. If your Concentration breaks or you can't take the Magic Action, the Spell is countered, but you don't expend a Spell Slot.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text:
A Spell ends when its Duration expires. A Duration usually takes one of these forms:

A span of time The effect lasts a set number of Rounds, minutes, hours, or longer. You can end it at any time (no action required). Concentration A span of time marked (Concentration) lasts only while you maintain Concentration. Until dispelled The effect has no time limit. You can still end it at any time (no action required). None (—) The effect resolves at once and doesn't persist.

docs.title: Concentration
docs.text:
Some Spells require Concentration to maintain. Your Concentration ends when any of the following occur:

Time limit If the effect has a maximum duration, your Concentration ends when that time passes. A second Concentration After you start Concentrating on another effect, you end one of them. Damage After you take damage, you make a Concentration Save to keep Concentrating. The DC equals 10 or half the damage taken (rounded down), whichever is higher, to a maximum of 30. Incapacitation Your Concentration ends after you become Incapacitated, Downed, or die.

After your Concentration ends, the effect you were concentrating on ends.

docs.title: Ending Early
docs.text: A Spell normally ends when its Duration expires. Other effects can also end a Spell early, either before or after the Spell takes effect.

docs.title: Countering
docs.text: When you counter a Spell, the Spell never occurs and produces no effects. A Spell can only be countered as it is being cast, and still expends its Spell Slot, Action, and any other costs, unless the effect that counters it says otherwise.

docs.title: Dispelling
docs.text: When you dispel a Spell, the Spell's effect ends before its Duration expires. A Spell can be dispelled by another effect, or by its own, and it can be dispelled on a few of its targets while continuing on others.

docs.title: Overlapping Spells
docs.text:
The effects of the same Spell cast more than once don't combine. Instead, the most potent effect from those castings applies while their Durations overlap.

The effects of different Spells add together while their Durations overlap. If multiple Spells have conflicting effects, the Spell with the highest level applies. If both Spells are the same level, the most recently cast Spell applies.

docs.title: Identifying Spells
docs.text:
While a Spell's effect is observable, you can Study to identify it, making an Arcana Check (DC 15). On a success, you learn the name of the Spell that created the effect.

Before a creature you can see casts a Spell, you can take that Study Action as a Reaction. After you do, you can use a second Reaction that triggers when the Spell is cast (no additional action required).

docs.title: Multiclass Spellcasting
docs.text:
If you gain the Spellcasting Feature from both your Primary and Secondary Classes, your Spell Slot capacity depends on your individual Levels in those classes. Spellcasting variants, such as Pact Magic and Sorcery, don't count toward multiclass Spellcasting.

Class Multiplier Artificer × ½ Bard × 1 Cleric × 1 Druid × 1 Fighter × ⅓ Paladin × ½ Ranger × ½ Rogue × ⅓ Wizard × 1

docs.text:
